pr_title: test_runner: reimplement `assert.ok` to allow stack parsing
pr_body:
Fixes #54760
Ref: https://github.com/nodejs/help/issues/4461

By default, `assert.ok` uses itself as a reference for where to start checking the stacktrace. In the test runner, there is a wrapper around this call (for `test.plan`), so it can't use itself as a reference.

This PR pulls out `innerOk` into it's own file, allowing the test runner to re-implement `assert.ok` using it's own function as a reference for the stacktrace.

(Hopefully that makes sense).

I've figured out a much less hacky way to acheive the same result.

I'm currently facing the following issue:
I've extended the stacktrace call-finding to search for the most recent userland function that called the assert. However, this causes the following case:
```
myEvent.on("event", assert);
myEvent.emit("event", false);
```

Will cause `myEvent.emit("event", false)` to be the error, not `true === false`. I'm not opposed to that behavior, but that changes the existing behavior, making this semver-major, so I want some feedback on that first? WDYT?

> making this semver-major

We should try to avoid that if possible.

> > making this semver-major
> 
> 
> 
> We should try to avoid that if possible.

We can go back to what it was, that is, reimplemented in the test runner, but it's kinda hacky.
The thing about semver major changes is not only that they are breaking and can cause users headaches, but they can't be backported, so Node 20 will have this bug until April of 2026.
It's also worth noting that bugs can have two "fixes." One that can be backported and one that cannot.
Got it. I'll fix the bug (backportable), and than make any non-backportable changes separately
Okay, the PR is back to how it was, with the hacky solution. I'll open a followup once this lands that is *not* backportable. This on the otherhand, is backportable.

issue_context.title: Assertion code parsing does not occur using TestContext's assert.
issue_context.body:
The following code snippet:

```mjs
import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert';

await test('foo', t => {
  assert.ok("Hello" === "World");
});
```

Produces the following output:

```
      at Test.runInAsyncScope (node:async_hooks:211:14)
      at Test.run (node:internal/test_runner/test:887:25)
      at Test.start (node:internal/test_runner/test:786:17)
      at startSubtestAfterBootstrap (node:internal/test_runner/harness:280:17)
      at async file:///repro.mjs:4:1 {
    generatedMessage: true,
    code: 'ERR_ASSERTION',
    actual: false,
    expected: true,
    operator: '=='
  }

ℹ tests 1
ℹ suites 0
ℹ pass 0
ℹ fail 1
ℹ cancelled 0
ℹ skipped 0
ℹ todo 0
ℹ duration_ms 41.578387

test at repro.mjs:4:7
✖ foo (27.753865ms)
  AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: The expression evaluated to a falsy value:
  
    assert.ok("Hello" === "World")
  
      at TestContext.<anonymous> (file:///repro.mjs:5:10)
      at Test.runInAsyncScope (node:async_hooks:211:14)
      at Test.run (node:internal/test_runner/test:887:25)
      at Test.start (node:internal/test_runner/test:786:17)
```

Notice how the error message includes the failing assertion `assert.ok("Hello" === "World")`.

In contrast, the following code snippet:

```mjs
await test('foo', t => {

});
```

review_comments: This should go in the `lazyAssertObject()` function and not duplicate the logic for tracking the plan.
assert.ok needs it's own function, as it uses itself as the reference point for tracking the stacktrace. If it went in that function, it would have another wrapper around it, breaking that?
It shouldn't? Doesn't "needs it's own function" just mean that `ok` is passed as the first argument to `innerOk`?

Yes, `ok` is passed as the first argument, but if it's created in the `lazyAssertObject` function, the `get assert()` will make a new wrapper around `assert.ok` for test planning, meaning the function passed to `innerOk` isn't the same as the function that is exposed to the user (the wrapper).
That's frustrating. Please leave a comment that this is a hack and hopefully it can be revisited in the future.

I've added a TODO comment for this logic to be implemented via better handling in the `innerOk` function. How does it look?

I have an idea of how to implement that in the `innerOk`, and I'll try to set it up when I get a chance.

Why not pass `args` directly?
```suggestion
        innerOk(ok, args);
```
I implemented this the same way it is in the `assert` function, but I can change it if you'd like
IMO we should change to what I suggested, I assume the assert function is like that only because it's exposed and we can't make breaking change to it without a deprecation cycle.
